[{:db/id 17592186198272 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c3a2b291-c6dd-58c8-a10f-d851511d7bfc" :knowledge-point/title "Sketching Cartesian Products in the Coordinate Plane"}] :question/problem "Sketch a representation of the set $S = \{1, 2\} \times (0, 1)$ in the Cartesian plane." :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S = \{1,2\} \times (0,1)
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is either $1$ or $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S=
\Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in \{{\color{red}{1}},{\color{blue}{2}}\},\, y\in (0,1) \Big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_1\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}{1}}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S_1 = \Big\{ ({\color{red}{1}},y) \: : \: y \in(0,1) \Big\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/56/56f200fce557749a56b9b5b51bc670da5f8c7f2cdb0196392ee80efcd6be980a.png)

Next, consider $S_2\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{blue}{2}}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S_2 = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{2}},y) \: : \: y \in(0,1) \big\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/f9/f96074cc265bba6eb59717364d2aa5390fdccea4d398fe5ae0b99f7ad82f0b93.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S = S_1\cup S_2
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=[-1,1]\times \{-1,1\}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is either $-1$ or $1.$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in \{-1,1\}\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/3e/3ed05ffc58aad1a6c75e7862c1175f497fb14870e6650cc6c4ce01c3df091d8b.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1$

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/0f/0f57920b2532177b0d64ac3dc95feb6a476bb385112d736d702895862e7de2b2.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S = \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S=
\Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z,\, y\in \mathbb N\Big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_1\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any integer number and whose $y$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}{1}}.$

$$
S_1 = \Big\{ (x, {\color{red}{1}}) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z\Big\}.
$$

We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/6b/6b63e973bbcc3e25d601a1f6cef97f5a00cc22e738c46d04a1ac06851421894e.png)

Next, consider $S_2\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any integer number and whose $y$-coordinate equals ${\color{blue}{2}}.$

$$
S_2 = \Big\{ (x,{\color{blue}{2}}) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z\Big\}.
$$

We can represent $S_2$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f2/f24ce8f7610d096c795a8a74b0b714b720c36442042c28b66432d6b2102fb9d4.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3,S_4,S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup {S}_{4}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S=[-1,1]\times [0,1]
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in [0,1]\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{0}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $0$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
{S}_{0}=\{(0,y)\,:\,y\in [0,1]\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/1c/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general ${S}_{i}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some $i\in [-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
{S}_{i}=\{(i,y)\,:\,y\in [0,1]\}
$$

For each $i\in [-1,1],$ ${S}_{i}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,1).$

![](images/49/494c9d77b0ff339b90792270c9d641054a03a2918e3c56a93747b42a77ee3ccf.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I=[-1,1]:$

$$
S={⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}.
$$

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}:$

the Cartesian plane?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S=[-1,0]\times [-1,1]
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,0]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,0],\,y\in [-1,1]}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{0}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $0$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
{S}_{0}={(0,y)\,:\,y\in [-1,1]}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/c9/c93f3ad399b88ccbaac990f8f73e93cfdcb1192f52b9b12f2d3ce178776fa13b.png)

Now, consider a general ${S}_{i}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some $i\in [-1,0]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
{S}_{i}={(i,y)\,:\,y\in [-1,1]}
$$

For each $i\in [-1,0],$ ${S}_{i}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $(i,-1)$ to the point $(i,1).$

![](images/65/6557201d202a401a92ee37c9a69eab9ab6ab87c6342dbb9d2afebae30141346f.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I=[-1,0]:$

$$
S={⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}.
$$

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}:$

:question/problem "Let $I=[1,2]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,2-i]\times {i}.$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=1,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{1}=[0,2-1]\times {1}=[0,1]\times {1}={(k,1)\,:\,k\in [0,1]}.
$$

This represents a horizontal line segment from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](images/dd/ddb7039dfcdbc2ef4070ce732c635a48194b6675cc3c78de6267e656c5e8387a.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,2-i]\times {i}={(k,i)\,:\,k\in [0,2-i]}
$$

is the horizontal line segment from the point $(0,i)$ to the point $(2-i,i).$ 

![](images/e8/e83644a2f0de96ee58ea893028bb7a42681ee71a15d194f2b344c4c15f60fafe.png)

There are no points that lie in all sets. $$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=1,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{1}=[-1,1]\times [-1,1]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [-1,1],b\in [-1,1]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(-1,-1),$ $(-1,1),$ $(1,1),$ and $(1,-1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

$$
{X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times [-1,1]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [-i,i],b\in [-1,1]\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(-i,-1),$ $(-i,1),$ $(i,1),$ and $(i,-1).$

17592186199077 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199560 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $A$ and $B$ are sets, the Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs $(a,b)$ whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A \times B = \big\{(a, b) \: : \: a \in A,\, b \in B \big\}
$$

Many Cartesian products have natural representations in the Cartesian plane. The most common of these is the Cartesian product $\mathbb R^2{:}$

$$
\mathbb R^2 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y) \: : \: x,y \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

This infinite set contains all ordered pairs $(x,y),$ where $x$ and $y$ can be any real numbers. In other words, $\mathbb R^2$ contains every point in the Cartesian plane! 

![](images/07/070389fcdb6d69f9aa90dabbd98a0d3461e26d3e3e08b1d53b92e99688c09923.png)

Similarly, the set

$$
\mathbb R^3 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y, z) \: : \: x,y,z \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

describes every point in three-dimensional Cartesian space. 

![](images/e7/e74fb5948144bc61173e4de73865cb746278bd31fd87e4abf927fa01821ba936.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "c18e6618-573b-5560-8d95-58ed56f05155" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c7652427-e5ff-5d02-9f23-39039f090aff" :step/math-academy-id 153383 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199078}} {:db/id 17592186199078 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198272 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198169 :question/id #uuid "bb40c174-3739-50df-835e-5d47c9902d5b" :question/math-academy-id "e-13192"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c3a2b291-c6dd-58c8-a10f-d851511d7bfc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048899} {:db/id 17592186050367} {:db/id 17592186050432} {:db/id 17592186050763} {:db/id 17592186050923}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198802} {:db/id 17592186198807} {:db/id 17592186287775} {:db/id 17592186287870} {:db/id 17592186287871} {:db/id 17592186389895} {:db/id 17592186390326} {:db/id 17592186421830} {:db/id 17592186422996}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching Cartesian Products in the Coordinate Plane"} :step/id #uuid "2190f1df-5853-5d8c-85e2-33f40f1f0f24" :step/math-academy-id 153384 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199079}} {:db/id 17592186199079 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199579 :tutorial/content "Cartesian coordinates can also be used to visualize other Cartesian products.

For example, let's consider the following Cartesian product:

$$
\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^- = \big\{(x,y) \: : \: x\in\mathbb N,\, y\in\mathbb R^-\big\}
$$

This product contains every point in $\mathbb R^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is a negative real number.

To visualize this Cartesian product, consider the following subset of our Cartesian product:

$$
S_1 = \big\{ (1,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f6/f6165f66b4149b7b2ea52a3cd686836853d85048ca890e850cb771174a150c57.png)

Next, we consider the subset $S_2,$ given by

$$
S_2 = \big\{ (2,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-.
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. 

![](images/ca/caf2299a2e8009ad5b2776ce67786fa7c7e3bdb57aacbd7df87882f59a2350e2.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3, S_4, S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}N\times {R}^{-} & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-$ as the set of vertical rays shown in the diagram below.

![](images/03/033c40b86bfd5cebf24d34de644f632213207386c2b67c559af7594468599e1e.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "1626e562-8e88-5ff3-bae3-4162438c0086" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8329 :tutorial/title "Cartesian Products of Countably Infinite Sets"} :step/id #uuid "cd371945-c79b-5b78-9017-15c39e4d5ed7" :step/math-academy-id 153387 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199080}} {:db/id 17592186199080 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198273 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198154 :question/id #uuid "eae94514-cd92-5405-90b1-ee09dad18e13" :question/math-academy-id "e-13162"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2aee319-68d6-54f7-8023-b24d32610bc4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050088}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198778} {:db/id 17592186198779} {:db/id 17592186287749} {:db/id 17592186287752} {:db/id 17592186287753} {:db/id 17592186287777} {:db/id 17592186287784} {:db/id 17592186287787} {:db/id 17592186389909} {:db/id 17592186389916} {:db/id 17592186422995} {:db/id 17592186506559}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane"} :step/id #uuid "48b1fb46-7071-5897-9dd7-a47e1d955f6c" :step/math-academy-id 153388 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199081}} {:db/id 17592186199081 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199584 :tutorial/content "Let's sketch a representation of the set $S= [0,1] \times [0,1]$ in the Cartesian plane.

The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S = [0,1] \times [0, 1]
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S=
\big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in [0,1],\, y\in [0,1] \big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_0 \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}0}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{red}0} = \big\{ ({\color{red}{0}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

We can represent $S_{\color{red}0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/1c/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general $S_{\color{blue}{i}} \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{blue}{i}} = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{i}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

For each ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1],$ $S_{\color{blue}{i}}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $({\color{blue}{i}},0)$ to the point $({\color{blue}{i}},1).$

![](images/28/28b9aa0559635ed4090f10dd0b59f2cbb6c297f8736d9509a637b5d78d27561c.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I = [0,1]{:}$

$$
S = \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}.
$$

As $\color{blue}i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union $\displaystyle \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}{:}$

$$
S_1 = \big\{ (1,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f6/f6165f66b4149b7b2ea52a3cd686836853d85048ca890e850cb771174a150c57.png)

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}N\times {R}^{-} & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$

The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S = [0,1] \times [0, 1]
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S=
\big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in [0,1],\, y\in [0,1] \big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_0 \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}0}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{red}0} = \big\{ ({\color{red}{0}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

We can represent $S_{\color{red}0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/1c/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general $S_{\color{blue}{i}} \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{blue}{i}} = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{i}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

For each ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1],$ $S_{\color{blue}{i}}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $({\color{blue}{i}},0)$ to the point $({\color{blue}{i}},1).$

![](images/28/28b9aa0559635ed4090f10dd0b59f2cbb6c297f8736d9509a637b5d78d27561c.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I = [0,1]{:}$

$$
S = \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

![](images/4d/4d0fe261e790520e6a8786e6f024d5b9cb7cd54c18242103a1f4b77f09653abc.png)

$$

$$

$$

![](images/1c/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

$$
{S}_{i}=\{(i,y)\,:\,y\in [0,1]\}
$$

$$
S={⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}.
$$

$$
S=[-1,1]\times \{-1,1\}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is either $-1$ or $1.$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in \{-1,1\}\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}
$$

![](images/3e/3ed05ffc58aad1a6c75e7862c1175f497fb14870e6650cc6c4ce01c3df091d8b.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1$

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/0f/0f57920b2532177b0d64ac3dc95feb6a476bb385112d736d702895862e7de2b2.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

$$

In this case, the set 

$$

$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in Z,\,y\in R\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(-1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/3f/3fdfed680e3fb46adbe8a70aac86682aacb85d43e0675923f87658635fc89a1e.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/7f/7fbda500ecca7e18c9db9939ad78d4dcc6bf488bc7fc4de1137e764ce21a0254.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}… \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $Z\times R$ as the set of vertical lines shown in the diagram below.

and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=R\times Z
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a real number and whose $y$-coordinate is an integer number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in Z\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1.$

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/8e/8e677c814756c4818c25da450d789c974787df60cf4bb18017a96593d3ecc180.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f9/f99beeb00c070048ee4ee7c1b6c9e077d7d4e0f3fd9e63aa12b5b58588e14dbb.png)

We can create the subsets $…{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{0},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times Z & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times Z$ as the set of horizontal lines shown in the diagram below.

$$
P(x)=2x^3 -6 x^2 + 8
$$

The degree ($n=3$) is odd and the leading coefficient ($a_3 = 2$) is positive. Therefore, the polynomial has the following end behavior:

- $P(x)$ approaches $-\infty$ as as $x$ approaches $-\infty.$

- $P(x)$ approaches $\infty$ as $x$ approaches $\infty.$

Only the graph $\textbf{C}$ satisfies these conditions."} {:db/id 17592186050294} {:db/id 17592186129672 :question/id #uuid "48aecd52-4119-5d5f-bc4a-b9f7c2052f44" :question/math-academy-id "q-38586"} {:db/id 17592186129678 :question/id #uuid "0a195ea9-9030-592b-a61d-ebfc1a12796b" :question/math-academy-id "q-38611" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129142 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5dce1c69-c79d-541a-b479-8fc127352c2a" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Graph of a Polynomial"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c673febf-2343-532e-b3f8-d17144d07bb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "A" :db/id 17592186127550} {:answer/id #uuid "d61ae7a1-00bb-5f11-ad1d-b0434b01b6c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None of the given options is correct" :db/id 17592186127551} {:answer/id #uuid "e412493d-069b-51b7-a259-1b98f29e80ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "B" :db/id 17592186127552} {:answer/id #uuid "efd3f6e9-8c99-5bdf-b917-997aad0d4a98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "C" :db/id 17592186127553} {:answer/id #uuid "082c4fa3-468a-5f61-8c9b-166620b0d5a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "D" :db/id 17592186127554}] :answer-field/id #uuid "5176cfc6-698c-5192-a037-61627dd873dc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186127549}] :question/problem "![](images/43/43e2c01d6e2ee22fe666bbaa46586b43467f8dd580d76e4da6644ac845761d31.png)

- $-2 x^4 + 6 x^3 - 2 x^2 - 6 x + 4$

- $-2 x^5 + 6 x^4 + 5 x^3 - 2 x^2 - 3 x + 1$

- $3 x^4 + 5 x^3 - 2 x^2 - 3 x - 4$

- $- x^4 + 5 x^3 - 2 x^2 - 3 x - 1$" :question/worked-solution "Let's call $P(x)$ the polynomial shown in the diagram.

The end behavior of $P(x)$ is

- $P(x)\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty,$ and

- $P(x)\to-\infty$ as $x\to \infty.$

Consequently, 

- the degree of $P(x)$ is even, and

- the leading coefficient of $P(x)$ is negative.

So, $P(x)$ is neither II nor III.

Lastly, note that the $y$-intercept is $4,$ which means that $P(0)$ must be equal to $4.$

Therefore, $P(x)$ is given by polynomial I."} {:db/id 17592186129669 :question/id #uuid "96dc2c59-fa2a-5c54-9157-5439d3af487c" :question/math-academy-id "q-38577"} {:db/id 17592186129680 :question/id 17592186129992 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130362 :tutorial/content "The **end behavior of a function** refers to what the function does when the input value $x$ is very large (either positive or negative).

For example, consider the polynomial $p(x)=x^2+2x+1.$ We can understand its behavior for very large $x$ by looking at its graph. 

![](images/61/61c2c4cd7efd64af7474bb8854b6d18878f5f5d932103f477d3048f806f83890.png)

Let's inspect the graph as $x$ becomes very large.

- As $x$ becomes very large in the *positive* direction, the polynomial $p(x)$ grows very large in the positive direction as well. So, we say that "the polynomial $p(x)$ approaches positive infinity as $x$ approaches positive infinity," and we write

$$
p(x) \rightarrow +\infty \quad \text{as} \quad x \rightarrow + \infty.
$$

- As $x$ becomes very large in the *negative* direction, the polynomial $p(x)$ again grows very large in the positive direction. So, we say that "the polynomial $p(x)$ approaches positive infinity as $x$ approaches negative infinity," and we write

$$
p(x) \rightarrow +\infty \quad \text{as} \quad x \rightarrow - \infty.
$$

We can confirm this by evaluating the function at large values of $x.$

- For large *positive* inputs, the values of $p(x)$ get larger.

$$
\begin{aligned} & p(100)={100}^{2}+2(100)+1=10\,000+200+1=10\,201 \\  & p(1\,000)=1\,{000}^{2}+2(1\,000)+1=1\,000\,000+2\,000+1=1\,002\,001\end{aligned}
$$

- For large *negative* inputs, the values of $p(x)$ again get larger.

$$
\begin{aligned} & p(-100)=(-100)^{2}+2(-100)+1=10\,000-200+1=9\,801 \\  & p(-1\,000)=(-1\,000)^{2}+2(-1\,000)+1=1\,000\,000-2\,000+1=998\,001\end{aligned}
$$

As you can see from the above computations, it is the leading term that "decides" the behavior of the function at infinity. 

In general, to determine the end behavior of a polynomial, all we have to do is look at the leading term. Let's see how to do this.

**Note:** The "$+$" sign is often dropped from the notation for positive infinity. Whenever you see an infinity symbol without a sign in front of it $(\infty),$ it means positive infinity $(+\infty).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "52110345-2f36-5b82-bbec-fd2652974cdd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3754 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c7aeb535-c560-542f-99a4-d820ea0fb077" :step/math-academy-id 21034 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130066}} {:db/id 17592186129993 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129142 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128958 :question/id #uuid "e6a96fc8-6ce5-5f47-8c20-709754ed7bc9" :question/math-academy-id "e-5811"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5dce1c69-c79d-541a-b479-8fc127352c2a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050294}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129672} {:db/id 17592186129678} {:db/id 17592186247239} {:db/id 17592186326700} {:db/id 17592186326701} {:db/id 17592186348327} {:db/id 17592186348328} {:db/id 17592186348330}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Graph of a Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "45634997-3461-5304-ba13-8e6c45c7966b" :step/math-academy-id 21036 :step/next {:db/id 17592186129996}} {:db/id 17592186129996 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130365 :tutorial/content "If you can't remember all the different cases, there's a trick you can use to determine the sign of infinity:

- Substitute $+1$ and $-1$ into the leading term of your polynomial and check the sign of the result.

- The sign of the result corresponds to the sign of infinity approached by the function for $x\rightarrow +\infty$ and $x\rightarrow -\infty,$ respectively.

To illustrate, consider the following polynomial:

$$
P(x) = 2x^3 -6 x^2 + 8
$$

Here, the leading term is $2x^3.$ Applying the trick, we have that

- $2(+1)^3 = {\color{blue}\mathbf+2},$ which indicates that $P(x) \rightarrow  {\color{blue}\mathbf +\infty}$ as $x \rightarrow +\infty.$

- $2(-1)^3 ={\color{red}\mathbf-2},$ which indicates that  $P(x) \rightarrow {\color{red}\mathbf-\infty}$ as $x \rightarrow -\infty.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a7432afa-735c-57a7-b142-14f04ddc4606" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3758 :tutorial/title "A Mnemonic Trick for Remembering the End Behavior Rules"} :step/id #uuid "6662a6a5-d337-5f20-831c-ac489c0a2202" :step/math-academy-id 21039 :step/next {:db/id 17592186129997}} {:db/id 17592186129997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129144 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128961 :question/id #uuid "7098a9a5-23ea-5496-a492-191c9c1a0690" :question/math-academy-id "e-5815"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ef7cf112-ab08-5e7a-855d-91bb69ec7f76" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129669} {:db/id 17592186129680} {:db/id 17592186247241} {:db/id 17592186247242} {:db/id 17592186326703} {:db/id 17592186348349}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Polynomial Given its Graph"} :step/id #uuid "22c9c4e6-e813-537b-b868-7519b78fd1af" :step/math-academy-id 21041 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130001}} {:db/id 17592186130001 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129148 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128962 :question/id #uuid "fdba6918-c9be-5a77-b79c-4a5cf39bf6e4" :question/math-academy-id "e-5817"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "34aa8f4e-20f1-5dda-ac53-6eb411543897" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129671} {:db/id 17592186129679} {:db/id 17592186247243} {:db/id 17592186326693} {:db/id 17592186326712} {:db/id 17592186402649}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements Regarding the Graph of a Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "f4fa3201-26b5-5053-8910-004a345d5b15" :step/math-academy-id 21047} {:db/id 17592186130066 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130395 :tutorial/content "In general, if we have a polynomial

- Substitute $+1$ and $-1$ into the leading term of your polynomial and check the sign of the result.

- The sign of the result corresponds to the sign of infinity approached by the function for $x\rightarrow +\infty$ and $x\rightarrow -\infty,$ respectively.

To illustrate, consider the following polynomial:

$$
P(x) = 2x^3 -6 x^2 + 8
$$

Here, the leading term is $2x^3.$ Applying the trick, we have that

- $2(+1)^3 = {\color{blue}\mathbf+2},$ which indicates that $P(x) \rightarrow  {\color{blue}\mathbf +\infty}$ as $x \rightarrow +\infty.$

- $2(-1)^3 ={\color{red}\mathbf-2},$ which indicates that  $P(x) \rightarrow {\color{red}\mathbf-\infty}$ as $x \rightarrow -\infty.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a7432afa-735c-57a7-b142-14f04ddc4606" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3758 :tutorial/title "A Mnemonic Trick for Remembering the End Behavior Rules"} :step/id #uuid "6662a6a5-d337-5f20-831c-ac489c0a2202" :step/math-academy-id 21039 :step/next {:db/id 17592186129997}} {:db/id 17592186130365 :tutorial/content "If you can't remember all the different cases, there's a trick you can use to determine the sign of infinity:

$$
f(x) = a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+...+a_{1}x + a_0
$$

with leading coefficient $a_n\neq 0,$ the end behavior of the polynomial is always

$$
f(x) \rightarrow +\infty \quad \text{or} \quad f(x) \rightarrow -\infty
$$

as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty.$ The sign of infinity depends on whether the leading exponent is even or odd, and on the sign of the leading coefficient. 

- If the leading coefficient is *positive*, then $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to +\infty.$ Otherwise, if the leading coefficient is *negative*, then $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to +\infty.$

- If the leading exponent is *even*, then the end behavior as $x \to +\infty$ is the *same* as the end behavior as $x \to -\infty.$ Otherwise, if the leading exponent is *odd*, then the end behavior as $x \to +\infty$ is *opposite* the end behavior as $x \to -\infty.$

The different cases are summarized in the table below.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{-t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ |  |

|  | $-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 4{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(-1+2\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(-1-2\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((-1+2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(-1+2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(-1+2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ (-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+2{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308656 :question/id #uuid "b84514fc-4c30-5d7a-9804-4a0f60502965" :question/math-academy-id "q-334631"} {:db/id 17592186308657 :question/id #uuid "f29b7109-5c33-5046-8236-7d693dea5b92" :question/math-academy-id "q-334634" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7805cc61-032d-5340-b315-43d00f9ec949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\operatorname{cos}(3t)-\operatorname{sin}(3t)" :db/id 17592186306291}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306291} :answer-field/id #uuid "5694d036-6e3a-56ea-beeb-680490a87b8c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307787} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aacf013a-2689-512b-8794-bcbacddaf843" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5\operatorname{sin}(3t)" :db/id 17592186306764}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306764} :answer-field/id #uuid "674d0fa8-85cf-5f7e-bdaa-2d7ca81bb93d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307849}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3\text{i}t) & ={e}^{3\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot 3\text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}.

{:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186308300}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $3t$ | $1-3t$ |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1+3t), \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3{e}^{3t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1+3t & -3t \\ 3t & 1-3t\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308671 :question/id #uuid "3361c13c-b482-5551-8d22-7ff3a0ff8596" :question/math-academy-id "q-334732"} {:db/id 17592186308672 :question/id #uuid "4bf1a0f0-bb87-5dac-ad3b-1ce93c87e2a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334733" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52b1d7ae-e4dd-5799-9115-e6e7b1fd12ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12t" :db/id 17592186305951}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305951} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dde19ef-9af0-5255-a3d4-655b000140c4" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307818} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fc7ea02-06bd-5e6c-aed2-4751d80186b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+6t" :db/id 17592186305289}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305289} :answer-field/id #uuid "893c4189-3f31-573e-94ae-26b874312a53" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307952}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{bmatrix}.$

|  | {{field-2}} | $1-6t$ |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =8{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1+6t) \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & =12{e}^{2t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1+6t & -3t \\ 12t & 1-6t\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308673 :question/id #uuid "05e36fef-5d87-510d-a2e4-12cce4dfd1e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334734"} {:db/id 17592186308674 :question/id #uuid "d74b37d0-1ddd-5304-877c-4617a1e8ae03" :question/math-academy-id "q-334735" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3cddbd6d-ffb7-5530-be33-109a25cb590f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-4t" :db/id 17592186305736}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305736} :answer-field/id #uuid "28239443-16fd-5045-bb7b-a3e946af529a" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307647} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6fff644e-a154-526d-b37a-e4f82a475e0e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2t" :db/id 17592186306218}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306218} :answer-field/id #uuid "6cec750e-1b50-5e87-b62d-239edf61a752" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307873}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -2 \\ 8 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$

|  | $8t$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -2 \\ 8 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 8{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2{e}^{3t}t \\  & ={e}^{3t}(-2t) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1-4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1+4t & -2t \\ 8t & 1-4t\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308675 :question/id #uuid "f4735ae9-8565-5d9f-a6c0-722d2b8017a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-334737"} {:db/id 17592186370138 :question/id #uuid "82844d09-60ab-554e-a1dc-5c9f8fec5040" :question/math-academy-id "q-334731"} {:db/id 17592186553504 :question/id #uuid "23c462cc-da9f-5356-aacb-68452f1af0c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334736" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8abba599-d405-5b28-8292-a43ed4750a5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2t" :db/id 17592186553149}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553149} :answer-field/id #uuid "03ccd2db-1552-543e-9102-8cfc8d2f158f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186553378} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f9e4d7af-e293-52fb-87b2-17e379489288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8t" :db/id 17592186553364}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553364} :answer-field/id #uuid "416cdcae-3262-544e-a6bf-81a343fec464" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186553403}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 \\ -8 & 2\end{aligned}].$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 \\ -8 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t)={e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-2t)={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}(-2t){\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-2t{e}^{-2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}(1+2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(2t) \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & =-8{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(-8t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1-4t & 2t \\ -8t & 1+4t\end{aligned}].

17592186222306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222473 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to compute the **matrix exponential**.

Recall that the scalar exponential function $e^t$ can be written as the power series 

$$
e^t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{t^k}{k!} = 1 + t + \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!} + \cdots.
$$

Now, let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix. By definition, the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ is given by the analogous series

$$
e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!} = I + tA + \dfrac{t^2}{2}A^2 + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!}A^k + \cdots.
$$

There are several approaches for computing matrix exponentials:

- The most direct approach is to use the definition above, but this is typically impractical.

- Another method, often covered in linear algebra courses, is to use the Jordan canonical form of $A$. This works, but it can also be tedious, especially for larger matrices.

Here, we will introduce a different method.

By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, every power $A^n, A^{n+1}, \ldots$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of 

$$
I, \: A, \: A^2, \: \ldots, \: A^{n-1}.
$$

As a result, $e^{At}$ can be written in the form

$$
e^{At}=\alpha_{n-1}A^{n-1} t^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1 At+\alpha_0 I,
$$

where $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-1}$ are functions of $t$ and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. 

Now, we define the polynomial 

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.
$$

Then we have the following key fact:

> For any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $At$, we have $r(\lambda) = e^{\lambda}.$

Let’s now see how this method works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "d78b3664-4117-56fc-bf30-5ca3acb28377" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f932ab79-9fa6-5a87-aa94-755b1685c4e3" :step/math-academy-id 588472 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222307}} {:db/id 17592186222307 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222482 :tutorial/content "Let's find $e^{At}$ for $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$ 

By solving the characteristic polynomial $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we can find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2, \qquad
\lambda_2=7.
$$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2t, \qquad
\lambda_2=7t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,\Rightarrow \,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
5t\alpha_1 = e^{7t} - e^{2t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{5t}\bigl(e^{7t}-e^{2t}\bigr).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $7$ and subtracting twice the second one, we get

$$
5\alpha_0 = 7e^{2t} - 2e^{7t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{5}\bigl(7e^{2t}-2e^{7t}\bigr).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((2{e}^{7t}-2{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & =-7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{7}{5}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((7{e}^{7t}-7{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 7({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) & 5{e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e5aa695-b237-54d4-9836-20514d70dc9e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14389 :tutorial/title "2x2 Matrices With Distinct Real Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "3c91134a-154b-5692-a2cc-fdc45c81af7e" :step/math-academy-id 588473 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222308}} {:db/id 17592186222308 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221408 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221150 :question/id #uuid "35a158c3-37b6-5123-ba90-1fd05218ce43" :question/math-academy-id "e-21271"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fee186e0-579f-5104-b0e1-50540abc0bdc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050001}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221925} {:db/id 17592186221994} {:db/id 17592186308532} {:db/id 17592186308533} {:db/id 17592186308644} {:db/id 17592186308645}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Real Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "ebe4cfdc-9e1a-577d-ad38-9d117b4cf820" :step/math-academy-id 588474 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222309}} {:db/id 17592186222309 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221409 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221151 :question/id #uuid "18064c11-63d3-599a-b504-7b589f46c3dc" :question/math-academy-id "e-21272"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a118fe4a-cd1f-52f7-aa33-59f5494e4905" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048305}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221932} {:db/id 17592186222002} {:db/id 17592186308654} {:db/id 17592186308655} {:db/id 17592186308656} {:db/id 17592186308657} {:db/id 17592186308658} {:db/id 17592186308659} {:db/id 17592186308660} {:db/id 17592186370129} {:db/id 17592186532679}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "ea0b2d60-3227-5e25-b6a9-171c0dc66319" :step/math-academy-id 588478 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222310}} {:db/id 17592186222310 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222481 :tutorial/content "Recall that the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ can be written as

$$
e^{At}=\alpha_{n-1} A^{n-1}t^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1 At+\alpha_0 I.
$$

If we define the polynomial

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0,
$$

then for any eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ of $At,$ we have

$$
r(\lambda_i) = e^{\lambda_i}.
$$

However, for *repeated eigenvalues*, we have the following additional fact:

> If $\lambda_i$ is an eigenvalue of multiplicity $k$ with $k>1,$ then 
> 
> 
> $$
> \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(\lambda ){|}_{\lambda ={\lambda }_{i}}={e}^{{\lambda }_{i}},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{\lambda }^{2}}r(\lambda ){|}_{\lambda ={\lambda }_{i}}={e}^{{\lambda }_{i}},\,…,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{k-1}}{\text{d}{\lambda }^{k-1}}r(\lambda ){|}_{\lambda ={\lambda }_{i}}={e}^{{\lambda }_{i}}\end{aligned}
> $$

Let's apply these facts to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "d7b15b25-b73f-5d5f-aa02-e4c1a5e9804e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14388 :tutorial/title "2x2 Matrices With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "855a741b-2bbe-5e04-b892-8d1d9c7d0e65" :step/math-academy-id 588481 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222311}} {:db/id 17592186222311 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221410 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221152 :question/id #uuid "40a6318a-a1c9-55f3-afdb-02b43891d7b5" :question/math-academy-id "e-21273"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0fd1d280-c768-5504-892e-a9a1948e1f1a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221933} {:db/id 17592186222003} {:db/id 17592186308670} {:db/id 17592186308671} {:db/id 17592186308672} {:db/id 17592186308673} {:db/id 17592186308674} {:db/id 17592186308675} {:db/id 17592186370138} {:db/id 17592186553504}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "de5a7d5c-0c01-5247-8ba6-a69a863c9cbb" :step/math-academy-id 588482 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222312}} {:db/id 17592186222312 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222505 :tutorial/content "Again, let $A$ be a constant $n\times n$ matrix. The matrix exponential satisfies

$$
\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\bigl(e^{At}\bigr)=A\,e^{At}.
$$

Indeed, recall that

$$
e^{At}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(At)^k}{k!}
=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!}.
$$

To prove the formula, we differentiate the series above term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}) & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}\cdot k{t}^{k-1}}{k!} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k-1}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{j=0}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{j}{t}^{j}}{j!} \\  & =A\,{e}^{At}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "739548ab-310c-5de3-a426-1fcaa3282478" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14526 :tutorial/title "Derivatives of Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "fc10fbf4-2be0-5b3f-ad2e-0505b175d5a6" :step/math-academy-id 588485 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222313}} {:db/id 17592186222313 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221411 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221194 :question/id #uuid "c0213c76-94e8-5ab3-a260-8a78a205589a" :question/math-academy-id "e-21724"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d4fc3ba4-d488-5156-88dc-837369269cef" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221995} {:db/id 17592186222006} {:db/id 17592186308726} {:db/id 17592186308727} {:db/id 17592186308728} {:db/id 17592186308729} {:db/id 17592186308730} {:db/id 17592186308731} {:db/id 17592186308732} {:db/id 17592186370312} {:db/id 17592186370321}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Derivative of a Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "df4956ab-0323-513e-ab21-66734987f4d0" :step/math-academy-id 588486 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222314}} {:db/id 17592186222314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222506 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials have other properties. We list a few of them:

- *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

$$
e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
$$

- *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

$$
(e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
$$

- *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

$$
e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
$$

- *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

$$
e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
$$

**Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute." :tutorial/id #uuid "2fcc3801-5d58-5c8e-b8c8-7be65b34f71a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14527 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "24b8ab46-a4b1-5358-abbd-db086f102dbf" :step/math-academy-id 588489}] :activity/title "Matrix Exponentials" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221467} {:db/id 17592186222306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222473 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to compute the **matrix exponential**.

where $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-1}$ are functions of $t$ and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. 

Now, we define the polynomial 

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.
$$

Then we have the following key fact:

> For any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $At$, we have $r(\lambda) = e^{\lambda}.$

Let’s now see how this method works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "d78b3664-4117-56fc-bf30-5ca3acb28377" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186222307 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222482 :tutorial/content "Let's find $e^{At}$ for $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$ 

By solving the characteristic polynomial $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we can find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2, \qquad
\lambda_2=7.
$$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2t, \qquad
\lambda_2=7t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,\Rightarrow \,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
5t\alpha_1 = e^{7t} - e^{2t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{5t}\bigl(e^{7t}-e^{2t}\bigr).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $7$ and subtracting twice the second one, we get

$$
5\alpha_0 = 7e^{2t} - 2e^{7t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{5}\bigl(7e^{2t}-2e^{7t}\bigr).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((2{e}^{7t}-2{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & =-7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{7}{5}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((7{e}^{7t}-7{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 7({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) & 5{e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e5aa695-b237-54d4-9836-20514d70dc9e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14389 :tutorial/title "2x2 Matrices With Distinct Real Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "3c91134a-154b-5692-a2cc-fdc45c81af7e" :step/math-academy-id 588473 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222308}} {:db/id 17592186222482 :tutorial/content "Let's find $e^{At}$ for $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$

The matrix exponential satisfies

$$
\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\bigl(e^{At}\bigr)=A\,e^{At}.
$$

Indeed, recall that

$$
e^{At}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(At)^k}{k!}
=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!}.
$$

To prove the formula, we differentiate the series above term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}) & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}\cdot k{t}^{k-1}}{k!} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k-1}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{j=0}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{j}{t}^{j}}{j!} \\  & =A\,{e}^{At}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "739548ab-310c-5de3-a426-1fcaa3282478" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14526 :tutorial/title "Derivatives of Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "fc10fbf4-2be0-5b3f-ad2e-0505b175d5a6" :step/math-academy-id 588485 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222313}} {:db/id 17592186222505 :tutorial/content "Again, let $A$ be a constant $n\times n$ matrix. We list a few of them:

- *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

$$
e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
$$

- *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

$$
(e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
$$

- *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

$$
e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
$$

- *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

$$
e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
$$

**Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute." :tutorial/id #uuid "2fcc3801-5d58-5c8e-b8c8-7be65b34f71a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14527 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "24b8ab46-a4b1-5358-abbd-db086f102dbf" :step/math-academy-id 588489} {:db/id 17592186222506 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials have other properties. *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $3t$ | $1-3t$ |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1+3t), \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3{e}^{3t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1+3t & -3t \\ 3t & 1-3t\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "03d5d0e2-58f6-580f-b08d-c488e5333a32" :step/next {:db/id 17592186532761}} {:db/id 17592186532736 :step/content {:db/id 17592186532679 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9a8db4e8-f732-5d22-9704-09e0ccf298b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\cos(3t)+\sin(3t)" :db/id 17592186532285}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186532285} :answer-field/id #uuid "3247c73e-d754-5617-80f3-a0beacefea90" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186532515} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f84eb7c6-9806-5d01-aade-ce5ce09883c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sin(3t)" :db/id 17592186532472}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186532472} :answer-field/id #uuid "4788b925-6ee1-5536-8ffa-a6478b71d51d" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186532525}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "900adaef-859d-5d14-9981-202d2269e069" :question/math-academy-id "q-334626" :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}].$

| ${e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\,\,$ |  | $3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ | $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3\text{i}t) & ={e}^{3\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot 3\text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5{\alpha }_{1}t & =-5\cdot \frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "783d8e6f-d461-5f0b-8f11-aa192fbe52a4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186532728}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7805cc61-032d-5340-b315-43d00f9ec949" :answer/type {:db/id $$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$

$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\text{i}t) & ={e}^{\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot \text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}

$$

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -{\alpha }_{1}t \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\text{i}t) & ={e}^{\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot \text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t & =-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & =\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "16872273-54fb-5073-a5e6-85ee3dbf9ea6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186553611}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7afe076b-ab10-5a6d-92ee-d9bda36095eb" :answer/type {:db/id |  | $8t$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -2 \\ 8 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 8{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2{e}^{3t}t \\  & ={e}^{3t}(-2t) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1-4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1+4t & -2t \\ 8t & 1-4t\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "30faf73f-f8c2-56a2-805f-6ce1667a314c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186553678}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3cddbd6d-ffb7-5530-be33-109a25cb590f" :answer/type {:db/id
